entities.summary:
Julius II was the Pope of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 1503 until his death in 1513. Born into the powerful Borgia family, Julius II was a key figure in the High Renaissance, patronizing artists such as Michelangelo and Raphael. He played a central role in the Italian Wars, leading the Papal States against the French and Spanish empires.

 As a leader, Julius II was known for his military prowess and strategic thinking. He expanded the Papal States, negotiating the Treaty of Perpiñan in 1503 and the Treaty of Bologna in 1504. These treaties secured the Papal States' borders and established a period of relative peace.

 Despite his military successes, Julius II's papacy was also marked by controversy and power struggles. He clashed with the French king Louis XII, who sought to expand French influence in Italy. Julius II's papal name was often seen as a reference to Julius Caesar, and his legacy continues to be debated among historians.

 The legacy of Julius II can be seen in the many artistic and architectural achievements of his papacy. The Sistine Chapel, which Julius II commissioned from Michelangelo, is one of the most famous works of art in the world. The Pazzi conspiracy, a plot to overthrow Julius II, led to the establishment of the Medici dynasty in Florence. The papacy of Julius II also saw the rise of the Counter-Reformation, a movement aimed at suppressing Protestantism and other heresies.

 In the years following his death, Julius II's reputation as a warrior pope continued to grow. He was seen as a symbol of the Catholic Church's power and influence during a tumultuous period in European history.
